---
title: "Training zones"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4.6, dpi = 110, out.width = "100%")
library(lactater)
plex <- requireNamespace("systemfonts", quietly = TRUE) &&
  isTRUE(suppressMessages(systemfonts::require_font("IBM Plex Sans", fallback = "sans")))
if (plex) options(lactater.font = "IBM Plex Sans")
```

Two thresholds split the intensities of an athlete into three *domains*, each with its own physiology ([Jamnick et
al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-020-01322-8); [Hofmann & Tschakert, 2017](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2017.00337)):

* **Moderate**, below the first threshold (LT1): lactate stays near resting values.
* **Heavy**, from LT1 to the second threshold (LT2): lactate is higher but can still reach a steady state.
* **Severe**, above LT2: lactate finds no steady state and keeps rising until the athlete stops.

LT2 methods aim at the maximal lactate steady state (MLSS). Some physiologists put the heavy/severe boundary at the
critical power instead, which in a meta-analysis sat 12 W above the MLSS on average, with 95% limits of agreement from
-19 to 44 W ([Jones et al., 2019](https://doi.org/10.14814/phy2.14098); [Micheli et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.19060)), so treat the top of the heavy domain as approximate.

`lactate_zones()` places the zone boundaries at these domain boundaries, so every zone belongs to one domain, and
colors the zones by domain: green for moderate, yellow for heavy, red for severe.

Zones anchored to the athlete's own thresholds hold up better than fixed percentages of a maximum. In 100 adults the
lactate threshold fell anywhere between 45 and 74% of V&#775;O<sub>2max</sub> and the MLSS between 69 and 96%, so the same
percentage put different people in different domains ([Iannetta et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1249/MSS.0000000000002147)). Across 42 training studies in healthy,
mostly sedentary or untrained adults, training set from thresholds raised V&#775;O<sub>2max</sub> more than training set from
percentages of a maximum: 4.1 against 1.8 mL/kg/min in the studies with a control group ([Meyler et al.,
2025](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-024-02125-x)).

## Choose LT1 and LT2

You decide which thresholds mark LT1 and LT2, and the choice matters. A review of the methods found that LT1 has
some evidence for separating the moderate and heavy domains, with Log-log and Bsln+ 0.5 among the most defensible,
and that few methods have evidence for separating the heavy and severe domains: Bsln+ 1.5 estimated the maximal
lactate steady state in two studies with 3-min stages, and Log-Poly-ModD<sub>max</sub> in one study with 4-min stages ([Jamnick
et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-020-01322-8); [Jamnick et al., 2018](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0199794)). With 3-min stages in elite cyclists, D<sub>max</sub> and the Stegmann IAT were
within 5 W of the MLSS, while ModD<sub>max</sub> and OBLA 4.0 overestimated it by 32 and 43 W ([Płoszczyca et al.,
2020](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13102-020-00219-3)); with 4-min stages in men of mixed fitness, the IAT of lactater was 37 W below it ([Hauser et al.,
2014](https://doi.org/10.1055/s-0033-1353176)).

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(lactater)
library(dplyr)

results <- demo_data |>
  lactate_threshold(intensity, lactate, heart_rate, plot = FALSE)

## the heavy domain (zone 2) for four pairs of LT1 and LT2
tribble(
  ~lt1, ~lt2,
  "LTP1", "LTP2",
  "Log-log", "Log-Poly-ModDmax",
  "Bsln + 0.5", "Bsln + 1.5",
  "OBLA 2.0", "OBLA 4.0"
) |>
  mutate(heavy = purrr::map2(lt1, lt2, \(a, b) {
    lactate_zones(results, lt1 = a, lt2 = b) |>
      slice(2) |>
      select(heavy_from = intensity_from, heavy_to = intensity_to)
  })) |>
  tidyr::unnest(heavy)
```

On the same test, the heavy domain starts anywhere from 83 to 111 W and ends anywhere from 118 to 160 W, depending
on the pair. Report the pair you used, and keep it between tests of the same athlete.

## Three zones

Zone 1 is the moderate domain, zone 2 the heavy domain, and zone 3 the severe domain, as in the three-zone model of
[Hofmann & Tschakert (2017)](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2017.00337):

```{r, fig.height = 7}
zones <- lactate_zones(results, lt1 = "Log-log", lt2 = "Log-Poly-ModDmax")
zones
autoplot(zones)
```

Each zone comes with its intensity, the lactate on the fitted curve, and, when given, the heart rate and RPE. Heart
rate and RPE at a boundary are interpolated between the stages, and extrapolated from the first three stages when a
boundary lies below the first stage.

With heart rate in the test, the plot shows it in a panel under the curve, on the same intensity axis, with its value
at LT1 and LT2. Many lab reports draw it on the lactate plot against a second axis instead; `heart_rate = "axis"` does
that, and `options(lactater.heart_rate = "axis")` does it for every plot and report. Where the two lines cross on such
a plot depends only on how the two axes are scaled, so read the heart rate from its own axis, not from the crossing.

```{r}
autoplot(zones, heart_rate = "axis")
```

## Five zones

The five-zone scale used in endurance sports ([Seiler, 2010](https://doi.org/10.1123/ijspp.5.3.276)) maps onto the domains: zones 1 and 2 lie below LT1, zone
3 between LT1 and LT2, and zones 4 and 5 above LT2, as the training of 11 Olympic and world champions was described
([Tønnessen et al., 2014](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0101796)). `model = 5` builds these zones from your two thresholds:

```{r, fig.height = 7}
five <- lactate_zones(results, lt1 = "Log-log", lt2 = "Log-Poly-ModDmax", model = 5)
five
autoplot(five)
```

No published five-zone scale is built on individual thresholds alone. Their lactate and heart-rate limits are group
averages: Seiler's scale, for example, puts zone 3 at 2.5 to 4 mmol/L, while lactater's zone 3 is this athlete's own
heavy domain. Other five-level scales put LT1 at a different cut altogether ([Jamnick et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-020-01322-8), Table 1), so check
which scale a coach means. The cut inside each domain is a convention, set with `split`:

* `"equal"` (default): zone 1|2 at half of LT1, and zone 4|5 halfway between LT2 and the highest intensity of the test.
* `"seiler"`: where the fitted curve reaches 1.5 mmol/L (zone 1|2) and 6.0 mmol/L (zone 4|5), the lactate limits of
  Seiler's (2010) scale. A cut outside its domain, or never reached, falls back to the equal split, with a warning.
* Two intensities of your own, `c(zone 1|2, zone 4|5)`.

```{r}
splits <- list(equal = "equal", seiler = "seiler", own = c(70, 175))
splits |>
  purrr::imap(\(split, name) {
    lactate_zones(results, lt1 = "Log-log", lt2 = "Log-Poly-ModDmax", model = 5, split = split) |>
      summarise(split = name, zone_1_2 = intensity_to[1], zone_4_5 = intensity_to[4])
  }) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()
```

Only the cuts inside the moderate and severe domains move; the domains themselves stay where LT1 and LT2 put them.

## Heart rate and RPE in the zones

Zones are often prescribed by heart rate or RPE. With both recorded, every zone gets a range for each. This client's
RPE is simulated (see `?lactate_tests`):

```{r}
client_results <- lactate_tests |>
  filter(test == "untrained") |>
  lactate_threshold(intensity, lactate, heart_rate, rpe_column = rpe, plot = FALSE)

lactate_zones(client_results, lt1 = "Log-log", lt2 = "LTP2") |>
  select(zone, intensity_to, heart_rate_from, heart_rate_to, rpe_from, rpe_to)
```

Two cautions. Heart rate lags behind intensity in short intervals, so heart-rate zones suit steady efforts better
than intervals ([Seiler, 2010](https://doi.org/10.1123/ijspp.5.3.276)). And RPE at a threshold varies between people and between tests: in 2,560 adults, RPE
was 10.8 at the last intensity before lactate began to rise and 13.6 at 1.5 mmol/L above it (Dickhuth's individual
anaerobic threshold), each with a standard deviation of 1.8 ([Scherr et al., 2013](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-012-2421-x)). Use it as a cross-check of the zones, not as their definition.

## Why not seven zones?

lactater leaves seven-zone models out for now. We found no seven-zone model anchored on individual lactate
thresholds, and the top zones of the scales with more than five zones are defined by how long an effort can last
(about 4 min, 1 min and 15 s to exhaustion for the top three zones of the eight-zone Olympiatoppen scale;
[Olympiatoppen, 2024](https://olt-skala.nif.no/olt_2024_en.pdf)), which a step test does not measure.
